public_rationale: There is evidence for parts of the criticism. [The Leaderboard Illusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879) identifies preferential evaluation and distorted scores, while [Microsoft's marketing](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/blog/2024/09/16/microsoft-365-copilot-wave-2-pages-python-in-excel-and-agents/) combines future promises with selected present-day claims. The benchmark operator disputes important findings. These records do not establish the broad causal claim that intentional future-product selling drove the industry's favorable descriptions instead of actual outcomes.
limitations: The benchmark dispute concerns a specific platform.
Marketing content establishes what a company said, not why journalists adopted particular descriptions.
The claim's breadth and causal language require more than isolated examples.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Because AI labs and hyperscalers intentionally sold their products on a theoretical future version that would fix all the problems, their 'powerful AI', graded on preferential anecdotes and rigged benchmarks rather than actual outcomes, was always described as 'on the frontier' and 'getting smarter every day'.

statement.excerpt: Their “powerful AI” — graded not based on actual outcomes but preferential anecdotes and performance on benchmarks rigged for the LLMs — was always “on the frontier” and “getting smarter every day,” all because AI labs and hyperscalers had intentionally sold their products based on some theoretical future version that would fix all the problems.
statement.document_title: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands

from_speaker: graded not based on actual outcomes
some theoretical future version that would fix all the problems
our_interpretation: Assess the proposed causal connection between future-capability marketing, preferential evaluation, and favorable descriptions.
Read 'rigged' as deliberate selection or design that inflates the impression of capability. Ordinary benchmark limitations alone do not establish rigging.
Treat 'always' and 'all because' as a broad account of industry promotion, not a requirement to disprove it with one contrary adjective.
Use early 2023 through publication, following the surrounding historical discussion.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence links deliberate future-capability selling and preferential evaluation to the favorable descriptions across a representative set of labs, hyperscalers, and coverage.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence directly undermines the asserted dominant causal explanation, showing that the relevant descriptions were substantially grounded in demonstrated outcomes rather than the alleged promotional mechanism.

evidence.explanation: The study identifies selective disclosure, unequal testing opportunities, and score distortion in one prominent benchmark. It supports a narrower concern about preferential evaluation, not the entire claim about intentional industry marketing and its effects.

evidence.locator: Response to the claim that pre-release testing can boost Arena scores
evidence.explanation: The operator disputes the size and persistence of the alleged advantage while announcing clearer policies and provisional scoring. This is material counterevidence to treating benchmark rigging as an uncontested finding, though it is an interested-party response.

evidence.locator: Opening section, paragraph discussing customer feedback and product updates
evidence.explanation: The sales material combines promised improvements and selected customer examples with claimed current performance measurements. It demonstrates promotional framing but does not establish independent validity, promises to fix every problem, or influence on subsequent coverage.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A documented sample connecting specific future-capability pitches and manipulated evaluations to subsequent coverage, with evidence of intent and consideration of competing explanations.
